demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Dates or anniversaries connected to the event
avoid anything that could be stressful
I go over and over the details of the event trying to make sense of it

Threat.value: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places
Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen
Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

Memory.value: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to

Negative Appraisals.value: I can no longer trust my own body
The person I have become is unrecognisable to me
I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Magical Thinking: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad
issues.explanation: The denial/minimisation in Magical Thinking sits awkwardly with the very global, entrenched negative self-change appraisals. A patient who mainly copes by telling himself the event did not really happen or was not that bad would not typically also report such strongly elaborated identity-collapse appraisals unless there were clearer supporting items linking the trauma to guilt/shame; here the combination feels internally strained.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable.
issues.explanation: For trauma type 'accidentally caused serious injury to another', the negative appraisals are missing the expected guilt/responsibility/being dangerous-to-others theme. Instead they focus on global misery and identity change, which is not impossible but is a weak fit to the trauma-specific cognitive content.

vignette:
Mateo was an HVAC technician, a job he had once loved for its clean logic and tangible results. Now, at twenty-two, he found himself sitting in a therapist's office, describing a life that felt like it belonged to someone else. The person he had become since the accident seven months ago was, in his own words, completely unrecognisable to him. The accident itself was a moment of physics he now replayed endlessly. He was on a routine commercial rooftop job, the summer air thick with the smell of hot tar and the faint, chemical tang of refrigerant. He was hoisting a new compressor motor into place when his grip, slick with sweat, simply failed. The motor, heavy and dense, slipped from his grasp, twisted in the air, and fell over the edge. The silence that followed the sickening thud from the alley below was the most terrifying sound he had ever heard. His co-worker, Miguel, had been down there, packing up tools.

In the weeks that followed, the memory of that silence began to haunt him. It would find him in his quiet apartment at night, making him feel as though something terrible was about to happen again. The memory itself was no longer just a thought; it was an invasion. It would force its way into his mind while he was driving or trying to watch TV, bringing with it the phantom smell of hot tar. When these intrusions happened, his heart would hammer against his ribs and a cold sweat would break out across his skin, a visceral echo of the panic he felt in that moment. This constant state of threat seemed to be a magnet for the memory; the more on-edge and unsafe he felt, the more the images and smells of that day would ambush him, creating a vicious, repeating loop of fear.

Over time, Mateo's interpretation of the event, and of himself, began to harden into a set of painful certainties. He had come to believe that his own body was fundamentally unreliable, a traitor that could betray him at any moment. This conviction was tangled with a profound and unshakeable guilt; he would never forgive himself for what he saw as a failure to do more, to have held on tighter, to have shouted a warning he didn't have time to form. These beliefs coloured the memory itself, making it feel strangely alien, as if he were watching a film about a clumsy, negligent stranger rather than recalling something that had happened to him. The person in that memory, the one who let the motor fall, was not someone he could recognise as himself.

This crushing self-appraisal began to dictate his every move. Believing he was untrustworthy and incapable, he started to systematically dismantle his life to avoid any possibility of a repeat failure. He began turning down any job that involved heights or heavy lifting, making excuses to his dispatcher about a sore back. He stopped going out with friends, convinced he couldn't handle the stress of a noisy bar or the unpredictability of a conversation. His world shrank until it consisted only of his apartment and the simplest ground-floor service calls. This retreat into what he hoped would be a safe zone only served to amplify his sense of ambient threat; the outside world now seemed fraught with unmanageable risks, and even the silence of his own home felt menacing.

His avoidance, meant to protect him, became the very thing that cemented his negative self-view. Each job he refused was fresh evidence that he was no longer the competent technician he once was, reinforcing the feeling that he was an unrecognisable shadow of his former self. He spent his evenings alone, trapped in his apartment, going over and over the details of the accident, searching for a different outcome in the past that he could never change. This constant overanalysis only deepened his guilt. The upcoming seven-month anniversary of the accident loomed in his calendar, a date he dreaded with a sick intensity. It was this feeling-of being trapped in a shrinking room with a memory that wouldn't fade and a version of himself he couldn't stand-that finally led him to seek help. He was terrified of losing his job, but what frightened him more was the realisation that he was slowly losing himself entirely.
